name: Sukarno
info: Sukarno was an Indonesian nationalist who spent over a decade in Dutch detention, declared Indonesia's independence with Mohammad Hatta on 17 August 1945 and served as its first president until Suharto displaced him in 1967.

facts.born: 6 June 1901 in Surabaya, East Java, Dutch East Indies, originally named Kusno Sosrodihardjo; son of Raden Soekemi Sosrodihardjo, a Javanese primary school teacher and priyayi, and Ida Ayu Nyoman Rai, a Balinese Hindu of the Brahmin caste
facts.died: 21 June 1970 in Jakarta Army Hospital of kidney failure, while under house arrest; buried in Blitar, East Java, next to his mother
facts.role: Leader of the Indonesian National Party (from 1927); head of the Investigating Committee for Preparatory Work for Independence (1945); first president of Indonesia, 1945 to 1967, elected president for life by the MPRS in 1963 and stripped of the title in 1967
facts.known: the Indonesian independence movement; the Proclamation of 17 August 1945; Pancasila; Guided Democracy; the Bandung Conference and the Non-Aligned Movement; the campaigns over West Irian and against Malaysia; his fall after the events of 1965

t: Sukarno led the nationalist movement against Dutch rule, spent over a decade in Dutch detention, and with Mohammad Hatta declared Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945, after which he led the resistance to Dutch re-colonisation until recognition in 1949.

In 1959 he replaced a quarrelling parliamentary system with the authoritarian Guided Democracy, and in the early 1960s he pursued an aggressive foreign policy while the economy deteriorated and the Communist Party grew under his protection.

After the 30 September Movement of 1965, General Suharto took control, between 500,000 and over 1 million people were killed in the purge that followed, and Sukarno spent his last years under house arrest.
dyk: In his speech of 1 June 1945 Sukarno set out five principles, known as pancasila, that he saw as shared by all Indonesians; the version put into effect in the 1945 Constitution omitted the reference to Islamic law that an earlier draft had carried.
ev: Sukarno is born in Surabaya, in the Dutch East Indies
He and friends from a Bandung study club found the Indonesian National Party, and he becomes its first leader
At his trial in Bandung he delivers the speeches published as Indonesia Accuses and is sentenced to four years in prison
The Dutch governor-general sends him without trial into internal exile, first on Flores and from 1938 at Bengkulu
Sukarno and Hatta proclaim Indonesian independence on 17 August, and the next day Sukarno is elected president
He hosts the Bandung Conference of Asian and African countries
He restores the 1945 constitution by decree and begins Guided Democracy
Under the order known as Supersemar he transfers most presidential authority to Suharto, and he is placed under house arrest the next year

sections.early:
Sukarno was born on 6 June 1901 in Surabaya, East Java, in the Dutch East Indies. His father, Raden Soekemi Sosrodihardjo, was a Muslim Javanese primary school teacher and priyayi from Grobogan, Central Java; his mother, Ida Ayu Nyoman Rai, was a Hindu Balinese of the Brahmin caste from Buleleng. He was originally named Kusno Sosrodihardjo and, following Javanese custom, was renamed after surviving a childhood illness. His name comes from Karna, a hero of the Mahabharata. Like many Javanese, he had only one name.

After a native primary school he attended a Dutch primary school in Mojokerto, and in 1916 a Dutch-type secondary school in Surabaya, where he met Tjokroaminoto, a nationalist and founder of Sarekat Islam. In 1920 he married Tjokroaminoto's daughter Siti Oetari. In 1921 he began to study civil engineering, with a focus on architecture, at the Technische Hoogeschool in Bandung and received an engineer's degree in 1926. He was fluent in several languages, among them Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, Indonesian and Dutch. As a student he came to despise both traditional Javanese feudalism, which he considered backward and to blame for the country's fall under Dutch rule, and the imperialism of Western countries, which he termed the exploitation of humans by other humans. He blamed it for the poverty and low levels of education of Indonesians.
sections.rise:
Living under Tjokroaminoto, Sukarno was first exposed to nationalist ideas. In Bandung he read European, American, nationalist, communist and religious political philosophy and developed what he styled Marhaenism, named after a peasant he met who owned and worked his own small plot. He organised a study club, the Algemeene Studieclub, against the student clubs dominated by Dutch students. On 4 July 1927 he and friends from the club founded the Indonesian National Party (PNI), and he was elected its first leader. It advocated independence, secularism and unity among the ethnic groups of the Indies, and opposed imperialism and capitalism. After the failed communist rebellion of 1926 the party drew many university-educated young people.

Dutch agents infiltrated his meetings, and he was arrested on 29 December 1929. At his trial in Bandung in 1930 he made long speeches attacking colonialism, titled Indonesia Menggoegat (Indonesia Accuses). He was sentenced to four years in Sukamiskin prison, but press coverage and pressure from liberals in the Netherlands and the Indies led the governor-general to shorten the term, and he was released on 31 December 1931 as a popular hero. The PNI had split in his absence, and in 1932 he became head of Partindo, which favoured immediate mass agitation, against Hatta's and Sutan Sjahrir's slower strategy of educating a leadership. He was arrested again on 1 August 1933, and the governor-general used emergency powers to send him into internal exile without trial, to Ende on Flores in 1934 and to Bengkulu in 1938.
sections.deeds:
The Japanese invaded the Indies in 1942 and released the nationalist leaders. Sukarno chose to cooperate, wanting to use the Japanese to gain independence, and he headed mass organisations the Japanese set up that promoted recruitment of romusha, the forced labourers sent to build railways and airfields, and the requisitioning of food. Food requisitioning caused a famine on Java that killed more than one million people in 1944 and 1945; in Sukarno's view these were necessary sacrifices for future independence, and in later years he was lastingly ashamed of his part in the romusha. On 1 June 1945 he presented pancasila to the committee preparing independence: nationalism, internationalism, democracy, social justice and belief in God. On 17 August 1945, after youth leaders had pressed him to act on the Japanese surrender, he and Hatta proclaimed the Republic of Indonesia, and the next day Sukarno was elected president.

He then sought recognition abroad rather than battle with British and Dutch forces. Two Dutch military offensives, in July 1947 and December 1948, were followed by international pressure, and the Netherlands transferred sovereignty on 27 December 1949. As president he organised the Bandung Conference in 1955 and, in 1961, helped found the Non-Aligned Movement at Belgrade. In 1959 he reinstated the 1945 constitution by decree, and from 1960 he built his government on Nasakom, a union of nationalism, religion and communism. He had a hand in designing monuments and the Gelora Bung Karno sports complex.
sections.opponents:
The parliamentary years from 1950 were unstable. Darul Islam rebels refused his authority, and in 1957 regional military commanders in Sumatra and Sulawesi took over local government. He declared martial law in March 1957, nationalised 246 Dutch companies and expelled 40,000 Dutch citizens. Presidential Directive No. 10 of 1959 banned commercial activities by foreigners in rural areas; it targeted ethnic Chinese, and approximately 100,000 chose to return to China. The PRRI-Permesta rebels who formed in 1958 received money and weapons from the CIA, and were militarily defeated by the end of 1958.

Under Guided Democracy he disbanded parliament in 1960 and replaced it with one half of whose members he appointed, and with military backing disbanded the Masyumi party and Sjahrir's PSI. Opponents from Sjahrir to the Islamic politicians Mohammad Natsir and Hamka were imprisoned, and critical newspapers were closed. Vice President Hatta, who opposed guided democracy, resigned in December 1956. In 1963 the assembly elected Sukarno president for life, and a personality cult grew around him. Opponents attempted to kill him several times, including a grenade attack in 1957 in which six children were killed. His confrontation with Malaysia from 1964 and his withdrawal from the United Nations in January 1965 were opposed by elements of the military. The economy was neglected: money printed to pay for military spending produced inflation above 600% a year in 1964 and 1965, and he was contemptuous of macroeconomics, unable and unwilling to offer practical solutions.
sections.last:
By 1965 the PKI had three million members and Sukarno had approved the Communist Party chairman Aidit's call for a fifth armed force of peasants and workers. Before dawn on 1 October 1965 a group calling itself the 30 September Movement kidnapped and murdered six senior army generals. Major General Suharto took control of the army, and by 2 October the movement had failed. The army, together with the organisations Muhammadiyah and Nahdlatul Ulama, led a purge of communists and leftists, and the worst massacres were in Java and Bali. The most widely accepted estimates are that at least half a million were killed, and the lede gives between 500,000 and over 1 million; as many as 1.5 million were imprisoned at one stage or another. Sukarno referred to the generals' killings as a ripple in the sea of the revolution and failed to protect the PKI.

Students demonstrated against him from January 1966. On 11 March 1966 he signed the Presidential Order known as Supersemar, which assigned Suharto to take all measures considered necessary for security and stability. Whether he was forced to sign, perhaps at gunpoint, is a point of historical debate. Suharto had the PKI banned and arrested officials loyal to Sukarno. Sukarno relinquished his executive powers on 20 February 1967, and on 12 March 1967 the MPRS stripped him of the title of president for life and the MPR named Suharto acting president. He was held under house arrest, where his health deteriorated for lack of adequate medical care, and died on 21 June 1970.
sections.legacy:
Sukarno is called the Father of Proclamation (Bapak Proklamator). Under Suharto his role in the independence struggle was minimised and his name largely removed from public discourse. As opposition to Suharto grew, and after his fall in 1998, public interest in Sukarno revived. His legacy as the founding father of Indonesia and a symbol of national unity and independence is widely respected by many Indonesians, often more so than Suharto's. The Soekarno-Hatta International Airport keeps the Dutch spelling of his name, which he insisted he wrote with a u. On 9 September 2024 the MPR revoked the 1967 resolution that had removed him from the presidency and barred him from politics, on the ground that there had been no trial to prove that he was responsible for the events of 30 September.

He is still fondly remembered for promoting the influence of newly independent countries, and that streets in Cairo and Rabat and a square in Peshawar bear his name. In the early 1960s his aggressive foreign policy raised tensions with Western powers, the economy declined and a personality cult grew. Some scholars have posited that Western fears of his plan for a rival to the United Nations, CONEFO, were an overlooked factor in United States support for Suharto's takeover. His daughter Megawati Sukarnoputri became the fifth president of Indonesia.

summary: Sukarno (1901–1970) led the Indonesian nationalist movement, declared independence with Hatta in 1945 and was the country's first president. His Guided Democracy and campaigns abroad ended in 1965, when Suharto took control and a mass purge killed at least half a million people.
references: John David Legge, Sukarno: A Political Biography (Archipelago Press, 2003)
notes: Birth name: the lede says 'born Koesno Sosrodihardjo', the Early life section 'originally named Kusno Sosrodihardjo'; the latter is used.
Death toll of 1965-66: the lede says 'between 500,000 and over 1 million', the body 'at least half a million', imprisoned 'as many as 1.5 million'. Both stated.
Supersemar: the article says whether Sukarno was forced to sign is debated; stated as such. Sukarno's reasons for being at Halim on 1 October are said to be unclear and left out.

Where the article gives the Dutch offensives: 'Operation Kraai' on 19 December 1948 is shortened to 'December 1948'. The article says Sukarno sent a telegram to Sjarifuddin to lead the emergency government (probably an error for Sjafruddin Prawiranegara); left out.
The Dutch trade-company nationalisation (246 companies, 40,000 expelled) is dated 'December 1957' in the article, and Directive No. 10 to 1959; both used as given.
The article says the 'Konfrontasi' objective was 'not, as some alleged, to annex Sabah and Sarawak'; left out of the text.

The passage on KGB and CIA blackmail attempts, the marriages, the honours and the architecture of the Preanger Hotel were left out for space; 'allegedly' material on the generals' coup being a 'CIA-influenced' plot is not stated.

The article says the Bandung Conference aimed at 'uniting ... into the Non-Aligned Movement' in 1955 and also that NAM was established in 1961 at Belgrade; the text keeps 1955 to the conference and 1961 to NAM.

'Sukarno himself ordered the house of the Proclamation demolished' is given without a reason and left out. The article states Sukarno's Japanese-era role in 'Pancasila' differently in two places (the Jakarta Charter of 22 June and the final version of 18 August); only the final version's removal of the sharia reference is not mentioned for space.
Facts 'role': the article says the MPRS elected him president for life on 18 May 1963 and stripped the title on 12 March 1967.
